messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Restrained): Feeling physically restrained or held down, Conflict: Confrontations, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Vignette:
When he began treatment at seventy-six, Mr. Tran asked to be called Minh. He was a slight, stooped Vietnamese American man who had spent years keeping his life narrow and predictable. He lived alone, had never married, and still worked part-time in a warehouse, where he preferred tasks that let him stay at the edges of the floor rather than in the middle of noisy exchanges between other workers. He described the event that stayed with him as something from much earlier in his life, before he came to the United States, when he was a civilian in a war zone. Even as an older man, he spoke about it in a way that made clear it was not a distant, blurred chapter. The memory was exact.

As Minh recounted it, he had been a young man when soldiers entered the area where he was living. There had been shouting, the abrupt crack of confrontation, and the confusion of people trying to understand who was being accused of what. He remembered being grabbed and forced down, his arms pinned so tightly that the pressure of another person’s hands and body weight became part of the memory itself. He could still describe the feel of rough ground under him and the panic of realizing he could not move. What remained just as sharply was the smell around him in that moment: sweat, dirt, and the dense, sour odor of men crowded together in fear and aggression. Around him, voices rose in anger. He remembered the terror of not knowing whether the confrontation in front of him would end with release or death. When he spoke of it now, he did not tell it like a general war story. He told it as a sequence of exact sensations, as if the scene were still preserved intact.

Over the years, Minh found that the memory did not return gradually or with any warning he could prepare for. A smell in the wrong place, a sudden argument, or the feeling of being physically hemmed in could bring the whole scene back at once. He described these moments as if the past “opened” without permission. If two men on the warehouse floor began arguing near him, especially if voices sharpened into confrontation, he would feel his chest seize before he had time to think. The scene from the war would come back full and detailed, not as an idea but as something immediate. Likewise, if he was carrying boxes through a narrow aisle and another worker brushed past him too closely, or if he had to squeeze between pallets and felt trapped for a second, he was no longer simply an older man at work. His body reacted to the old experience of being held down. Certain smells were especially potent. The mix of sweat, damp cardboard, and industrial dust in the warehouse could catch him off guard and return him instantly to that earlier scene.

When this happened, Minh said he became so overwhelmed by emotion that he had to stop whatever he was doing. At work he would set down a box and step away, pretending he needed water or the restroom. He could not simply push through it. The intensity felt too great, and he feared that if he stayed where he was, others would see something was wrong. Because of this, he had quietly shaped his routines around what he knew he could not tolerate. He timed his breaks to avoid crowded areas. He chose solitary tasks when possible. If tension started rising between coworkers, he found reasons to move to another section of the warehouse. These habits made him seem private and somewhat distant. Supervisors knew him as reliable but hard to approach, and over time he had become even more isolated from the few coworkers who had once tried to talk with him during lunch.

Outside work, his life had also grown smaller. He avoided busy gatherings where people might press close to him. If someone touched him unexpectedly, even in an ordinary way, he felt a jolt of alarm that was hard to explain. He had spent decades telling himself this was simply how he was now. Still, what frightened him most in recent months was how immediate the memory remained. He had come to believe that after so many years it should have faded, yet it still arrived with perfect detail and enough force to interrupt the present.

He finally sought help after an incident at the warehouse in which two younger men began yelling at one another near a loading area. Someone moved quickly behind him in the commotion and caught his arm to pull him aside. The combination of confrontation, the sudden grip, and the smell of sweat and dust brought the memory back so completely that he had to leave the floor. He sat in his car for a long time afterward, shaken and ashamed that he could not simply “be an old man going to work.” In asking for treatment, Minh said he wanted, above all, to be able to stay present when something in his surroundings reminded him of the past. What he feared most was that these moments would continue to overtake him without warning, leaving him trapped again in something he had survived long ago.
